Answer Keys Marks No. A fuel manufactured either from or by fresh, living micro- or macro-organisms or a fuel made directly or indirectly from biomass. Classification First Generation Biofuels Second Generation Biofuels Third Generation Biofuels Fourth Generation Biofuels 1A Merits 4 Biodegradability • Readily available feedstock • Environmentally and socially beneficial • Ensure energy availability • Extensive applications • Easy blending with petroleum-based fuel • Safe handling and transportation. Drawbacks Compete with food • Lead to the food vs. fuel debate • Growing of feedstocks requires large arable land and time • Agricultural inputs like fertilizer, herbicides, irrigation, and manpower required • Contribute the highest carbon footprint in comparison with other generations of biofuels. 1B 3 Cradle to Grave: includes the material and energy production chain and all processes from the raw material extraction through the production, transportation and use phase up to the product’s end of life treatment. Cradle to Gate: includes all processes from the raw material extraction through the production phase (gate of the factory); used to determine the environmental impact of 1C the production of a product. 3 Gate to Grave: includes the processes from the use and end-of-life phases (everything post production); used to determine the environmental impacts of a product once it leaves the factory. Gate to Gate: includes the processes from the production phase only; used to determine the environmental impacts of a single production step or process. 3 2A 4 2B 3 • From the Buswell equation: c=5, h=7, o=2, n=1 (s=0) • Note that in practice all ammonia (NH3) dissolves in the slurry. Therefore we only calculate CO2 and CH4 2C • C5H7O2N + {(4 × 5-7-2 × 2+3 × 1)/4} H2O → 3 • {(4 × 5-7+2 × 2+3 × 1)/8} CO2+ {(4 × 5+7-2 × 2-3 × 1)/8} CH4 • C5H7O2N + 3 H2O → 2.5 CO2+ 2.5 CH4 • The molar ratio for CO2 and CH4 is 2.5 : 2.5, thus the gas composition is 50% CO2 and 50% CH4 4 MEC technology is also known as biocatalysed electrolysis cells or electrofermentation. The MEC system has two electrodes, cathode and anode, which can either be placed in the same single chamber (single-chamber MEC) or be separately placed in two individual chambers (two-chamber MEC). In the two- chamber MEC, to separate the two chambers, commonly a proton exchange membrane is used. Other recently developed membranes include a charge-mosaic membrane, cation/anion exchange membrane and bipolar membrane. In the two- chamber MEC, the anode chamber is filled with the organic wastewater, while the cathode chamber can be filled with different solutions (like moderate acidified water, phosphate-buffered solution, bicarbonate buffers and salt solution. The main working process in both the MEC types is the same. Electrons get generated by the oxidation of organic matter in the anode, which are transported to the anode. Then, they are transported to the cathode where upon combining with protons, H2 gets generated. In addition to a potential generated by microorganisms (- 0.300 V), MEC needs a small external potential of more than 0.110 V for the production of H2. The external power source use of the battery is generally considered, but the use of renewable power generated from solar, wind, MFCs and waste heat can be seen. Anode:CH3COOH+2H2O→2CO2+8e-+8H+Anode:CH3COOH+2H2O→2CO2+8 e-+8H+ Cathode:8e-+8H+→4H2Cathode:8e-+8H+→4H2 3A 4 Overall:CH3COOH+2H2O→2CO2+4H2Overall:CH3COOH+2H2O→2CO2+4H2 Many different substrates were found in use for MEC to produce H 2. Some common pure chemical substrates used are butyrate, glucose, acetate and glycol. However, different waste streams like poultry farming wastewater, domestic wastewater, waste activated sludge and industrial wastewater are used in MEC. Raw materials, temperature, pH and operating voltage play an important role in determining the H2 yield in MEC. Definition BOD: BOD is the amount of oxygen consumed by bacteria while decomposing organic matter under aerobic conditions. COD: COD is the amount of oxygen required for the oxidation of total organic matter in water. 3B 3 Decomposition BOD: BOD is a biological oxidation process. COD: COD is a chemical oxidation process. Test Procedure BOD: BOD is determined by incubating a sealed water under specific temperature sample for five days and measuring the loss of oxygen from the 5 beginning of the test. COD: COD is determined by incubating a closed water sample with a strong oxidant like potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7 ) in combination with boiling sulfuric acid (H2SO4 ) under specific temperature for a specified period of time. Time Taken for Determination BOD: Five days are taken for the determination of the BOD. COD: COD measurement can be taken from few days.
